title: From a #4 country album to box fans
summary: Zac Kubilus produced Frank Foster's Rhythm and Whiskey, which reached #4 on Billboard's Top Country Albums in 2014. In 2016 he recorded a $15 box fan from Walmart and put it online. Today his top tracks are box fans, and Sleep Sounds is his full-time work.

Zac owns his recordings, his rights and his management, so he can try a new channel as soon as it opens. When Alexa arrived, Sleep Sounds became an Alexa skill. He explains why one owner now releases under three artist names after Amazon called "Sleep Sounds" too generic, and why the rules for functional audio now change in weeks or days instead of years.

We also cover whether AI companies should train on a catalog (his answer: it's up to the owner), whether an owner should train a model on recordings they own, Nashville writers demoing with Suno, whether AI output needs a label, and what selling direct has taught him that streaming didn't.

title: Nobody actually wants a marketing plan
summary: "Nobody actually wants a marketing plan," says Ali Lieberman, VP of Product at Symphonic Distribution. "They want the release to do well." That idea shaped the Release Campaign Builder, which Symphonic launched in February: a marketing plan built from a release's own data. Ali walks through one on screen, a demo release with a $500 budget and one goal, a playlist placement. One of Symphonic's senior A&R leaders called the output "annoyingly good."

Before Symphonic, Ali ran the US ISRC agency at the RIAA and improved business processes at SoundExchange. Her rule for AI comes from that work: it is "mostly an amplifier." Clean data and processes get faster; messy ones get you "amplifying mess." She explains which work Symphonic has handed to AI, how the team defines and tests those workflows, and what stays with people.

We also cover distributors as gatekeepers after UMG sued DistroKid and IFPI launched its Streaming Integrity Initiative, why the problem is "music pretending to be something that it isn't," why the default for AI training "should be no," and whether a model can price an advance: "I do not trust AI 100% to give the final number."

title: Buy at 8x, sell to fans at 20x
summary: "Our target multiple is a 20X," says Sean Peace, who founded SongVest in 2007. A catalog owner buys at 8x, then sells 10% or 15% of a song to fans at 20x. Fans pay it because a SongShare is "the coolest piece of memorabilia you'll ever buy": a piece of a song they love that actually pays a royalty.

We test that on one real offering. In SongVest's 2026 offering circular, a share of "Rain On Me" earned $12,637 over the last twelve months. The seller gets $252,750, about 20 times that, and fans pay up to $318,465, about 25 times. Sean explains who those buyers are, how payouts reach them, and why the first song he put on the marketplace, "Hit The Quan", was one he owned himself.

We also cover fewer, bigger buyers after Sony and Recognition and BMG and Concord, what drives a multiple a year later, why a ton of money doesn't make you good at valuing catalogs, why song shares don't trade like stocks yet, and what AI licensing will actually pay song owners.

title: Music licensing needs to be frictionless, not permissionless
summary: Jesse Kirshbaum signed the Clipse at 23. More than twenty years later, "Grindin'" is a Lavazza coffee. "Songs don't get old, but context is consistently changing," he says. That is his Living Catalog: brand partnerships that give older songs new meaning, and new income, long after the release date.

Jesse runs Nue Agency and writes the Beats + Bytes newsletter. He explains how a brand picks a song (data shows where the heat is, taste shows where it is going), why music licensing needs to be frictionless rather than permissionless, and what a label sitting on 5,000 songs should pitch first: not a playlist, a concept.
We cover Dolly Parton's Cup of Ambition coffee, DJ Khaled and Nesquik's "Another Bun", the 2025 NFL Draft walkout songs, Kid A Mnesia, and which archive deserves that treatment next.

title: AI music licenses will switch from market share to usage
summary: Vickie Nauman expects the first AI music licenses, signed on market share, to start paying on actual usage when they come up for renewal in one to two years. The founder and CEO of CrossBorderWorks has spent 26 years licensing new music technology, and she lays out what rights holders need before that switch: an attribution system for AI output, artist opt-in, and a transparency clause in every AI license.

We cover Spotify's AI artist badges, whether a Drake hit and a Kansas City singer-songwriter carry the same value in a training set, Merlin's role for independent catalogs, GEMA's court win against Suno, why AI-generated music should flow through the same DDEX pipes as everything else, and why 3.5 billion gamers make games a catalog income line. Vickie also explains why the industry lost four years trying to stop digital from 1999 to 2004, and why rights holders are at the table this time.

title: The $100K playbook of an independent artist
summary: Recorded in Miami during Art Basel 2024. Xcelencia runs his career the way a good company runs a product line: the album treated as software, distribution engineered through quests rather than playlist luck, and a direct commercial relationship with the collectors who fund the work.

We go through the numbers behind his $100K year, the tooling he built versus bought, token-bound accounts as fan infrastructure, and what he would keep if he started again. Required listening for anyone who owns a catalog and wants to see the leading edge of independent operation in practice.
